title: Vector Spaces, Subspaces, Span, Basis and Dimension
breadcrumb: Mathematics → Linear algebra → Vector spaces and dimension
engineName: Mathematics — independent directions and coordinate systems
objectives: Apply the subspace test to subsets of vector spaces.
Compute and interpret the span of a set of vectors.
Test linear independence using linear combinations or rank.

prereq.name: Vectors and linear combinations
prereq.why: Span and independence are defined through linear combinations.

traps: A non-homogeneous linear equation usually defines an affine set, not a subspace.
A basis must both span and be independent.
All bases of a finite-dimensional space have equal size.
The union of subspaces is not generally a subspace.

sheet: Subspace: non-empty, closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
One-step test: αu+βv∈W for all u,v∈W and scalars α,β.
Span{vᵢ}: all linear combinations; always a subspace.
Independent: only the trivial linear combination equals zero.
Dimension: number of vectors in any basis.
A line through origin is a subspace; a translated line is not.
Rank of a matrix equals dimension of its column space.
tricks: Check zero first when rejecting a proposed subspace.
Put spanning vectors as columns and find pivot columns.
Remove redundant vectors to obtain a basis.
Count basis elements, not the number of displayed generators.
Use the dimension formula to avoid constructing U+W explicitly.
shortcuts: Two independent vectors in R² form a basis.
Proportional non-zero vectors span a one-dimensional line.

howto: For a proposed subspace, check zero and closure. For a span or basis problem, put vectors into a matrix and use pivots to identify independent generators. Count the basis elements to obtain dimension.

scenes.title: Foundation: vectors and linear combinations
scenes.objective: Recall the algebra behind vector spaces.

ask.q: What is a linear combination of vectors v₁,…,vₖ?
ask.nudge: Multiply each vector by a scalar and add.

body: A vector space is a set with vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the usual axioms. Familiar examples include Rⁿ and polynomial spaces.
Span, linear independence, basis and dimension describe how vectors generate a space and how many independent directions it contains.

items.ask: What is the span of a set of vectors?
items.recall: All linear combinations of those vectors.
refresh: The span is the smallest subspace containing the given vectors. It always contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
If two vectors in R² are independent, their span is all of R². If they are proportional, their span is only a line through the origin.

items.recall: The only linear combination equal to zero has all coefficients zero.
refresh: A set is linearly independent if no vector in the set can be expressed as a linear combination of the others.
For a matrix with the vectors as columns, independence is equivalent to full column rank. This connects the abstract definition to row reduction.

items.recall: A linearly independent set that spans the whole space.
refresh: A basis gives every vector a unique coordinate representation. It has no redundant vectors, but it generates the entire space.
Every basis of a finite-dimensional vector space has the same number of vectors. That number is the dimension, so dimension is well-defined.

scenes.title: A basis is a minimal coordinate system

ask.q: Can a set span R² and still fail to be a basis?
ask.nudge: Yes, if it contains redundant vectors.

body: Spanning means there are enough vectors to reach every point in the space. Independence means none of the vectors is redundant.
A basis satisfies both. In R², two non-parallel vectors form a basis; three vectors may span R² but cannot be independent.

scenes.title: Subspaces and the subspace test
scenes.objective: Check whether a subset is a vector subspace.

ask.q: Is the set {(x,y):x+y=1} a subspace of R²?
ask.nudge: Does it contain the zero vector?

blocks.body: A non-empty subset W of a vector space V is a subspace if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.
W is a subspace iff it is non-empty and αu+βv∈W for every u,v∈W and scalars α,β.
Every subspace contains the zero vector. A line or plane not passing through the origin cannot be a subspace.

steps.why: The set is non-empty and contains zero.
The resulting vector has second coordinate twice the first.

scenario.teaser: A set of feasible parameter changes is closed under linear combinations.
scenario.title: Subspaces of allowable model perturbations
body: In a linear model, some parameter perturbations preserve a linear restriction. The set of all perturbations satisfying a homogeneous linear equation forms a subspace.
For example, y=2x describes a line through the origin. Adding two vectors on the line or scaling one vector keeps the result on the same line.
A non-homogeneous equation such as x+y=1 does not define a subspace because it excludes the zero vector. The homogeneous structure is essential.

scenes.title: Span and linear independence
scenes.objective: Determine whether vectors generate a space without redundancy.

ask.nudge: They are proportional and lie on the x-axis.

blocks.body: span{v₁,…,vₖ}={c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ:cᵢ∈R}. It is always a subspace.
The vectors are independent iff c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ=0 implies c₁=…=cₖ=0.
Place the vectors as columns of a matrix. They are independent iff the matrix has full column rank; row reduction identifies pivot columns.

scenes.title: Guided: find a basis for a span
scenes.objective: Remove redundant vectors from a generating set.
scenes.problem: Find a basis for span{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} in R².
hints: The first two vectors already generate every (x,y).
The third vector is the sum of the first two.
Keep only the independent generating vectors.
scenes.solution: The first two vectors are independent and span R². The third vector is redundant because (1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1).

ask.q: What is the dimension of this span?

scenes.title: Basis and dimension
scenes.objective: Connect basis size with the dimension of a space.

ask.q: What is the dimension of P₂, the polynomials of degree at most two?

blocks.body: The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the number of vectors in any basis.
dim(Rⁿ)=n. The polynomial space Pₙ of degree at most n has basis {1,x,…,xⁿ} and dimension n+1.
Relative to an ordered basis, every vector has a unique coordinate vector. Changing the basis changes coordinates, not the vector or the dimension.

scenes.title: Guided: polynomial coordinates
scenes.objective: Express a polynomial in a basis.
scenes.problem: Write p(x)=2−3x+4x² in the standard basis of P₂.
hints: Read the coefficient of each basis element.
Keep the coordinate order aligned with the basis order.
scenes.solution: p(x)=2·1+(−3)·x+4·x², so its coordinates in the ordered basis (1,x,x²) are (2,−3,4).

items.a: A non-empty subset closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
The set of all linear combinations.
The number of vectors in any basis.

scenes.title: Dimension counts independent directions

ask.q: Why does P₂ have dimension three rather than two?
ask.nudge: The constant, linear and quadratic terms are three independent directions.

body: Dimension counts independent directions, not the number of coordinates visible in a particular expression. P₂ contains polynomials with three independent coefficient choices.
The same idea applies to matrix spaces, solution spaces of linear systems and subspaces generated by data vectors. A basis gives the minimal number of coordinates needed.

scenario.teaser: A data set may contain many variables but fewer independent directions.
scenario.title: Dimension and redundant features
body: A data matrix may have many columns, but some columns can be linear combinations of others. The column space dimension is the rank, not the raw number of variables.
A basis selects independent columns that still span the same column space. The number of selected columns is the dimension of that space.
This is the geometric meaning of redundancy in a design matrix: the ambient number of variables can exceed the number of independent directions represented by the data.

scenes.problem: Find dim(U+W) when dim(U)=3, dim(W)=2 and dim(U∩W)=1.

steps.why: The intersection is counted in both dimensions and must be subtracted once.
The combined subspace has dimension four.

steps.math: The sum contains the directions in U and W without double-counting their common line.
steps.why: This is the finite-dimensional subspace dimension formula.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: Every subspace contains the zero vector.
items.why: It must be closed under scalar multiplication and non-empty.

items.claim: The set x+y=1 is a subspace of R².
The span of any set of vectors is a subspace.
items.why: Linear combinations are closed under addition and scaling.

items.claim: A basis must span and be linearly independent.
All bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same size.
items.why: This common size is the dimension.

items.claim: The union of two subspaces is always a subspace.
items.why: The union need not be closed under addition.

scenes.title: Final vector-space checklist
body: 1. Subspace: non-empty and closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
2. Every subspace contains zero; non-homogeneous affine sets usually fail this test.
3. Span is the set of all linear combinations and is always a subspace.
4. Independent means only the trivial combination gives zero.
6. Dimension = number of vectors in any basis.
